# What does the portal tell me?

*You'll need PnL as cash plus position (chapter 2) and a backtest's assumptions (chapter 6).*

## The story

In the Varde rehearsal (chapter 1), the first upload scored €367.61 on the three public sessions. Our backtest of the
same file, under its best guess of the exchange's rules, had said about €1,330, and calibrate, the tool
that searches our engine's settings for one that reproduces the portal, refused: no setting came within 5% of every
figure (@fig-calibrate).

So the session read the portal's results file by hand. The rules had said there was a fee per order placed as well as
per lot, and it was easy to underrate: the bot placed and cancelled orders all the time, and those fees came to €143 of
a €511 gross, **28%** [(`data/sessions.csv`; `python/experiments/mock_round/round4/README.md`)]{.src}. The fills file
showed a second gap: the portal had filled far fewer lots than any of our settings did (8,466 against 18,772 or
more). The rule behind it, that only half of each trade reached resting orders, was not stated; it sat in the
rehearsal's answer key. Neither was a strategy problem, and either would have misled every backtest that night
[(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/results/DRYRUN_LOG.md`, "What calibrate printed")]{.src}.

## The idea

### The twelve figures

An upload comes back with a dozen numbers. For the Varde upload:

| Figure | Varde upload | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `score` | 367.61 | the PnL that ranks you: cash plus the positions at the mark, less any penalty |
| `fills`, `tradedVolume` | 5,056; 8,466 | how many fills, and how many lots |
| `inventory` | −6 | the last session's end position, summed over products |
| `cash` | 2,310.30 | cash at the end, fees included |
| `markPrice` | 233.44 | the last session's marks, averaged over products |
| `breachPenalty` | 0 | the charge for going past a limit |
| `pnlSe` | 22.98 | the score's standard error |
| `absInventoryQ50` to `Q997` | 8, 13, 27, 36 | quantiles of the absolute position over the session |

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
The Varde upload came back with a score of 367.61 euros, 5,056 fills over 8,466 lots, an end position of minus 6, cash
of 2,310 euros, a mark price of 233.44 euros, no penalty, a standard error of 22.98, and an absolute position of 8 lots at the
median, 13 at the 68th percentile, 27 at the 95th and 36 at the 99.7th.
:::

Three of them repay a closer look.

**The score is an identity.** It is cash plus position times mark, as in chapter 2, less any penalty, and you can check
it. With one product and one session the check is exact. Here it fails twice over, and nothing is wrong: `cash` is
summed over all three sessions while `inventory` and `markPrice` are the last session's, and `markPrice` is one number
averaged over three products' prices. So 2,310.30 less 6 times 233.44 is not 367.61, and the identity holds only
session by session and product by product. Know which figures are sums before you compare them.

**`pnlSe` says how much the score is worth.** On the Varde portal it is the standard error of the total over the
sessions scored [(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/private/portal.py`)]{.src}:

::: {.eq speak="the standard error of a total over n sessions is the spread of the session scores times the square root of n"}
$$\text{pnlSe} = \text{sd}(\text{session scores}) \times \sqrt{n}$$
:::

The Varde sessions scored 110.21, 136.57 and 120.83: their spread is 13.3, times the square root of 3 is 23. Two
uploads whose scores differ by less than a couple of standard errors are not shown to differ, however tempting the
better number. With only a few uploads, this is what stops you chasing noise. What the Arena's `pnlSe` measures isn't known yet;
calibrate tries per-tick, per-block and per-day versions and keeps the one that fits.

**The position quantiles say how hard the bot leans on its limits.** The quantiles sum the position over products, and
the two products the bot traded allow 100 lots between them. A median of 8 lots and a 99.7th percentile of 36 mean the
bot is usually near flat and at most uses about a third of its room; a bot whose median is near its limit is carrying a bet,
whether it meant to or not.

### Calibrate: fitting the simulator to the real thing

Our backtest has a dozen settings that recorded data can't decide (chapter 6): which trades fill us, whether orders
rest and where they queue, delay, depletion, the mark, the share of each trade we can get. One upload of a plain bot
measures them. Calibrate replays the uploaded file under every combination, computes the same twelve figures, and ranks
the settings by their *worst* figure's error against the portal. If the best is within 5% on every figure, it prints the
settings to paste into the day's format. If not, it refuses, and names the usual causes: the money off by one factor (a
unit or scale mismatch), a cost the engine doesn't charge, or our wrapper doing something their exchange doesn't.

![Calibrate on the Varde upload: each figure's error, for the best-ranked setting and for the setting closest on fills
and volume alone, against calibrate's 5% line. Data: `data/calibrate.csv`, from `experiments.day.calibrate` through the
round's plug-in.](figures/f12_calibrate.png){#fig-calibrate
fig-alt="Dot plot of the error on eleven of the twelve figures (the penalty, zero on both sides, isn't drawn). The best-ranked setting is near 100% off on score, fills and volume. The setting closest on the fills is 2.6% off on fills and 10.5% on volume but 36% off on the score and over 300% on cash. Only the mark price is within 5% for both."}

@fig-calibrate shows why it refused. The best-ranked setting barely trades, which makes it "least wrong" on cash and
inventory and 98% wrong on the score. The setting closest on fills and volume, with half of each trade available, gets
fills within 2.6%, but it scores €236.58 against the portal's €367.61 and ends the last session with a different
position (−12 against −6), which throws cash off by over 300%. On top of
that, the order fee is a cost the engine can't charge at
all. No setting can be right everywhere when the exchange has rules the engine lacks, and a fit that is right on some figures
and wrong on others would have been worse than none.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
Calibrate is system identification: fit a simulator's parameters so that its outputs match logs from the real system.
Two things limit it. It sees twelve aggregate figures, not the hidden state, so very different settings can match the
same totals, which is why it ranks by the worst figure and not the average. And the simulator's family may not contain
the truth: refusing a bad fit is the same discipline as not deploying a model whose validation loss says it doesn't fit,
however good its best metric looks.
:::
